🛍️ Recontextualization

A Generative AI Interface for Contextual
Product Exploration and Evaluation

Jiin Choi1,†, Yugyeong Jang1,†, Haejoo Han2, Kyung Hoon Hyun1,*

1 Department of Interior Architecture Design, Hanyang University, Seoul, 04763, Republic of Korea

2 Department of International Business Administration, Dankook University, Yongin-si, 16890, Republic of Korea

† Equal contribution (co-first authors)* Corresponding author

TL;DR

Online shoppers need to connect a product’s appearance to the situations in which they intend to use it, yet expressing and exploring those situations can require repeated refinement. Recontextualization is a generative AI interface that turns a natural-language shopping query into recommended, editable tags for Actor, Motion, Scene, and Visual Background. These controls expose who is represented, what they are doing, where the product is used, and how the scene is presented. Shoppers can accept or revise the suggestions, regenerate contextual images using the original product image as a reference, revisit earlier variants, and compare selected products in a cart. Recommendations provide a starting point, while direct editing lets the imagined usage situation evolve.

We evaluated the interface through a video-based online experiment (N = 198) and an interactive laboratory study (N = 64). Compared with product-only imagery, the studies reported more favorable product attitudes or purchase intentions and higher perceived relevance and informativeness; the laboratory study also reported higher perceived customization and usability. Interviews and interaction traces describe how recommendations helped participants begin exploring and how editing supported more specific usage situations. These findings concern the integrated interface, rather than isolated features. Generated scenes support contextual imagination, but do not verify product dimensions or functional performance.

A backpack for your commute, a walk through the park, or a quiet moment outside. Recontextualization makes the situation around a product something you can inspect and change.

The idea

A shopping goal is a starting point.
Context gives it room to evolve.

Online shoppers connect a product to their own activities, surroundings, and preferences. Instead of asking them to express everything in a perfect prompt, the interface turns a broad goal into editable suggestions.

Start with a goal

Describe what the product is for. Recommended tags offer a concrete place to begin.

Make it your situation

Change who is represented, what they are doing, where they are, and how the scene feels.

Explore another possibility

Revisit earlier images and compare products across the contexts that matter to you.

Inside the interface

Search. Recontextualize. Compare.

A natural-language query becomes recommended tags. Shoppers can regenerate an individual product, inspect its image history, and bring selected items together in a cart to explore alternative situations.

How it works

A visible link between intent and imagery.

The system interprets a shopping query, recommends visual attributes, and translates them into four editable tags. A generation prompt combines those choices with the original product image as a reference.

Suggest

Propose a plausible starting context from the stated shopping goal.

Expose

Keep contextual descriptors visible and open to direct revision.

Refine

Generate another view while retaining a reference to the product under consideration.

What we learned

More relevant contexts.
More favorable product responses.

Two complementary studies compared the integrated interface with product-only imagery: an online video experiment and a hands-on laboratory study.

How to interpret these findings

The studies evaluate the integrated experience: contextual imagery, visual richness, and editing capabilities were bundled together. They do not isolate the effect of an individual feature. Purchase intention is self-reported, and mediation analyses do not establish a causal sequence among perceptions. The full paper discusses measurement, sampling, and generalizability.

A participant’s exploration

From a flight to the whole journey.

P13 was looking for a travel tumbler. During the session, they edited the Scene tag six times, expanding the imagined use from drinking on a plane to moving through a crowded airport and spending time at a destination. Editing the context helped them consider how different products might fit the broader travel experience.

“At first, I only thought about using it on the plane, but then I could consider airports and the entire travel situation.”

P13 · Expanding the imagined journey

Imagine a use. Then check the facts.

This example shows how one participant explored personally relevant situations. It does not establish that generated scenes improved decision accuracy or verified the tumbler’s physical properties.
